quote: Alle Gleichungen 4ten Grades mit rationalen Coefficienten und der Discriminante $\pm 1$ zu ermitteln. Zurückführen auf Gl. 3ten Grades, indem man die Darstell.
english: To determine all equations of the 4th degree with rational coefficients and discriminant $\pm 1$. Reduce to equations of the 3rd degree by [taking] the represent[ation]...
topic: Research notes listing three tasks: determining class numbers of multiquadratic fields (especially biquadratic fields), defining the lemniscate function by algebraic approximation following a hint by Gauss, and finding all quartic equations with rational coefficients and discriminant ±1.

triage.modern_statement: Find all quartic polynomials f(x) = a x^4 + b x^3 + c x^2 + d x + e (or binary quartic forms), most plausibly with rational-integer coefficients, whose discriminant is +1 or -1. The note suggests doing this through the associated cubic (the resolvent cubic, or the invariant/covariant representation of a quartic by a cubic). With rational coefficients that are not integers the question is trivial, since rescaling changes the discriminant freely, so the integral reading is the meaningful one. In modern terms this asks whether some quartic number field, or some quartic ring/order, has discriminant ±1.
triage.answered_by: This was settled in the negative for irreducible integral quartics by the Hermite–Minkowski theorem. Minkowski (c. 1890/91, Geometrie der Zahlen) proved Kronecker's conjecture that every number field other than Q has |disc| > 1. The discriminant of a monic irreducible integral quartic equals [O_K : Z[α]]^2 · d_K, so it can never be ±1. The same holds for irreducible integral binary quartic forms, because their discriminant is that of an associated quartic ring, which is an order in a quartic field. So no irreducible example exists. Only reducible cases with integer coefficients could remain, and I found no source treating Hilbert's specific formulation or his reduction to cubics.

evidence.claim: Minkowski's theorem: for n ≥ 2 the Minkowski lower bound exceeds 1, so every number field other than Q has a non-trivial discriminant.
Martinet notes that Minkowski's bound is greater than 1 for all n ≥ 2, which solves Kronecker's conjecture.
Mathlib formalizes the Hermite–Minkowski theorem: a nontrivial number field has |discriminant| > 1 (and indeed > 2).
Modern work counts integral binary quartic forms by their invariants, in the GL2(Z)-class framework, which is the setting of Hilbert's question.

triage.why: The note is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th. Under the natural integral reading, the question of which irreducible quartics have discriminant ±1 is answered, with none existing, by Minkowski's proof of Kronecker's conjecture. That proof dates from about the time Hilbert would have written this note. Nothing in the sources speaks to how Hilbert meant the reduction to cubics, whether he meant forms or monic polynomials, or the leftover reducible cases. Confidence is therefore medium, not high. Binary quartic forms in general are still actively studied (Bhargava–Shankar), but this specific question is not.
